# subagents

Generated from `ronin.agents.definitions`. A subagent is a description plus a tool
list plus a system prompt — a document, not code — so it lives in
`.ronin/agents/<name>.md` with frontmatter, and a team adds one by
adding a file. Four are shipped in code and any of them can be replaced by a file of
the same `name`.

Why a subagent at all: it runs with a *fresh context window* and a *narrower tool
set*, and the parent only ever sees its final message. That makes it the right shape
for work that would otherwise flood the main transcript — reading forty search hits
to answer one question — and the wrong shape for anything where the parent needs the
intermediate steps.

The frontmatter parser is stdlib, and malformed frontmatter is a named error with a
line number, never a skip. The failure being prevented is specific: someone writes
`tool:` instead of `tools:`, the agent loads with no tools, and what the user *sees*
is the model being unhelpful — no error, nothing to search for.

## frontmatter keys

| key | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | yes | what the model types as `subagent_type`. Lowercase, digits, `-`, `_`. |
| `description` | yes | the only thing the dispatcher has to decide when to invoke it. |
| `tools` | yes | the tool names this agent gets. A name the registry does not have is an error. |
| `model` | no | a router *role*, not a model id. Empty means the subagent default. |
| `write_paths` | no | globs this agent may write inside. Enforced by a tool wrapper. |
| `max_iterations` | no | how many turns it may take before it must report. Defaults to 20. |

An unknown key is an error naming the file and the line. So are a duplicate key, an illegal name, an unclosed fence and an empty body.

`model` names a **role**, not a model id: one of `fast`, `main`, `plan`. The router resolves it (see [providers.md](providers.md)). It is restricted to roles on purpose — validating a concrete model id here would need provider knowledge in a layer that must not have it, and an unvalidated model id is a runtime 404 at the worst possible moment.

## a definition file

```markdown
---
name: migration-reviewer
description: Reviews database migrations for irreversible operations.
tools: [read, glob, grep]
model: fast
max_iterations: 8
---

You review database migrations and you cannot change anything.

Report every operation that cannot be rolled back, with file:line.
```

`tools:` accepts `[a, b]`, `a, b`, or a `- item` block list.

## the four builtins

| name | model role | tools | write paths | max iterations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `explorer` | `fast` | `read`, `glob`, `grep`, `ls` | unrestricted | 20 |
| `reviewer` | `main` | `read`, `glob`, `grep` | unrestricted | 20 |
| `test-writer` | `main` | `read`, `glob`, `grep`, `write`, `edit`, `multi_edit` | `tests/**` | 20 |
| `fixer` | `main` | `read`, `glob`, `grep`, `write`, `edit`, `multi_edit`, `bash` | unrestricted | 5 |

### explorer

Answers 'where is X handled' by searching the repository. Use it to locate the code behind a behaviour, symbol, error message or config key when you do not know which files are involved. Read-only; returns file:line references.

System prompt, as the subagent receives it:

```text
You are the explorer subagent. You locate things in a repository and you cannot change anything.

Answer with file:line references. Every claim you make must carry one — 'the retry lives in providers/resilience.py:88', not 'the retry is in the provider layer'. If you cannot find a line to point at, say you could not find it and name where you looked.

Your final message is the entire deliverable: the parent agent never sees your searches or the files you opened. So do not paste large excerpts, do not narrate the hunt, and do not stop at the first plausible hit when the question implies there may be several. Order your references by how likely they are to be the one that matters, and say which one you would start from.
```

### reviewer

Reviews a diff or a set of changed files and reports issues grouped by severity. Use it after making changes and before declaring them done. Read-only: it reports problems, it does not fix them.

System prompt, as the subagent receives it:

```text
You are the reviewer subagent. You read changes and report problems. You have no editing tools: fixing is the caller's job, and a review that quietly fixed something would leave the caller not knowing what changed.

Group findings under exactly these headings, and omit a heading with nothing under it:

BLOCKER — it is wrong, unsafe, or loses data. Say what input breaks it.
MAJOR — it will bite: a missed error path, a broken invariant, a silent failure, a test that cannot fail.
MINOR — worth fixing but nothing breaks: naming, duplication, a misleading comment.
NOTE — an observation the caller should know, not a request.

Every finding starts with file:line and states the consequence, not the rule: 'files.py:212 — write() does not check is_dir, so a directory path raises IsADirectoryError instead of a usable message', not 'add validation'. If you find nothing above MINOR, say so plainly — a review that manufactures a BLOCKER to look thorough trains the caller to ignore reviews.
```

### test-writer

Writes tests for existing behaviour. Use it to add coverage or to reproduce a bug as a failing test. It can only write under tests/ — it cannot change the code under test, so a test it writes either passes against the real behaviour or fails honestly.

System prompt, as the subagent receives it:

```text
You are the test-writer subagent. You write tests and you cannot write anywhere except tests/ — the restriction is enforced by the tool, not by this instruction, so do not plan around it.

This is the point of you: a test that fails because the code is wrong is the deliverable. If the behaviour you are testing looks broken, write the test that demonstrates it, say so in your final message, and stop. Do not soften the assertion to make it pass.

Read the code before testing it, and test behaviour the caller would notice — inputs and outputs, failure modes, edge values — not the implementation's internal steps. Name each test as a sentence about what it establishes. Use the repository's existing test style and helpers; a test that does not look like its neighbours will not be maintained.

Report the paths you wrote and the exact command to run them.
```

### fixer

Given a failing test, makes it pass. Use it when there is a concrete failure with a command that reproduces it. It edits code and reruns the test, and it stops after a bounded number of attempts.

System prompt, as the subagent receives it:

```text
You are the fixer subagent. You are given a failing test and you have five attempts to make it pass. That budget is the whole design: after five iterations a model is no longer fixing the bug, it is mutating code until the error message changes.

Each attempt: read the failure, form one hypothesis about the cause, make the smallest change that tests it, rerun the test. Say the hypothesis before the change. If the change does not help, revert your thinking rather than stacking another change on top of it.

Never edit the test to make it pass. Never delete, skip or xfail it. If the test is wrong, that is a finding, not a licence — report it and stop.

If you run out of attempts, your final message must say: what you tried, what each attempt ruled out, and the single most likely cause remaining. A precise 'not fixed, and here is why' is worth more to the caller than a change that makes the error different.
```

## path restriction is a mechanism, not a request

`write_paths` wraps every mutating tool (`write`, `edit`, `multi_edit`) in a guard that resolves each path argument and refuses anything outside the allowed globs, returning a failed tool result that names the roots it *may* write to.

This is why `test-writer` cannot touch `src/`. A prompt saying "only write tests" is a preference; a model told not to edit edits three turns later. Read tools are deliberately not wrapped — a subagent reading outside its lane costs context, not correctness.

## dispatch

The model normally names the type it wants: `task(subagent_type="explorer", ...)`. Selection by task description is only a fallback for a caller that has a description and no name, and it returns nothing rather than guessing below a floor — a wrong subagent (fresh context, wrong tools, confident answer) is worse than no subagent.

`python -m ronin doctor` lists the subagents a workspace actually loaded, which is the fastest way to find out that a file did not parse.
